doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Writing 'Saint Michel' after the Paris subway bombing
summary: Asked how emotion becomes a composition, Ries describes writing the piece on a toy piano after a bombing in Paris he narrowly avoided.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: These circumstances from last night I got to hear a number of your original compositions and you seem to be affected by certain occurrences and then able to express your reaction to them in music, which you mentioned this incident about twenty years ago in Paris. When you sit — and you said there was a little piano after this subway incident. And I don’t know if you can describe how that emotion — probably shock — translates into a composition?

Well again I feel it’s just the music is there and you know whether it’s like I’m just capturing it and not getting in the way of it, which is kind of what happened in that situation where this song I wrote, the song “Saint Michel” which is based on that you know, 70 or so people being killed. And had it not been a beautiful day, if it had been raining I would have been on that train because it was so nice I’m going to walk. It’s going to take me an hour but I’m going to be outside, Paris the greatest city for walking maybe besides Rome. It’s like one of those places where you can get lost and spend hours just — oh let’s go down here. Just so thankfully it was a gorgeous day you know. But like knowing that that happened I got back to my friends, it literally was a toy piano the size of like the Linus thing, you know it was like maybe four octaves and it was out of tune
